title: Sequoia and OpenAI Back Harvey to Redefine Professional Services, Starting with Legal
author: Gabe Pereyra and Winston Weinberg (Harvey)

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core framing of Harvey as workflow infrastructure rather than a standalone drafting chatbot. It also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on whole-firm implementation, trust, security and review, while offering an aspirational company vision rather than evidence of durable adoption, competitive advantage or broader economic effects.
qs: At Harvey, we believe that the future of AI will not be a chatbot that compliments your workflow; it will be the platform your workflow is built on.
To empower both, Harvey must build the same trust by developing AI systems that are not only powerful, but also scalable, transparent, and secure.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition by presenting Harvey as infrastructure underlying legal workflows, built through firm-wide partnerships and trust mechanisms that preserve professional judgment. It also aligns with the cluster’s evidentiary caution: these are company ambitions and design claims, not measured proof of accuracy or productivity.
qs: At Harvey, we believe that the future of AI will not be a chatbot that compliments your workflow; it will be the platform your workflow is built on.

We do so by building systems that replicate historic best practices for establishing trust in knowledge work—such as tiered review and the ability to incorporate natural language feedback—while pioneering novel systems for AI alignment and validation.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the application-layer thesis by presenting Harvey as infrastructure for legal workflows rather than a chatbot, while treating trust, review and validation as necessary design conditions. Its claims are aspirational and promotional, with no measured evidence of performance or durable defensibility, consistent with the cluster’s qualification that traction and product ambition cannot establish a moat.

kp.k: Funding supports scaling Harvey's professional-services AI strategy
kp.d: In their April 26, 2023 company announcement, Gabe Pereyra and Winston Weinberg report a $21M Series A led by Sequoia, with participation from the OpenAI Startup Fund, Conviction, SV Angel and Elad Gil. They state that the funding provides resources to expand the team, deepen partnerships and develop AI systems for professional services; these are intended uses rather than demonstrated market effects.
qs: We are thrilled to announce our $21M Series A led by Sequoia with participation from the OpenAI Startup Fund, Conviction, SV Angel and Elad Gil.
The backing of our incredible investors gives us the resources to scale our team, deepen our partnerships, and build the AI systems that are the future of professional services.

kp.k: AI shifts knowledge work toward strategy, advice and judgment
kp.d: The authors present GPT-4 as a turning point in how professional services are delivered and consumed. They predict that large language models will handle complex tasks efficiently and accurately while leaving knowledge workers employed and more able to focus on strategy, advice and judgment. This is an augmentation claim, not an employment finding or a measured account of task performance.
qs: GPT-4 marks a shift in how professional services will be provided and consumed.
Large language models have the potential to give knowledge workers superpowers by solving complex tasks efficiently and accurately.

The best part: these solutions don't leave knowledge workers without work; they allow them to focus on the quintessential aspects of their professions—strategy, advice, and judgment—the exact work that makes the long hours, in school and at the job, worthwhile.

kp.k: AI becomes workflow infrastructure rather than a chatbot supplement
kp.d: Harvey's founders predict that AI will become the platform on which workflows are built, rather than an additional chatbot. They connect this vision to partnering with entire firms and learning from clients' actual problems, arguing that development must extend beyond training data and treatises. Their self-driving-car comparison serves as an analogy for the importance of development grounded in practice, not evidence of autonomous legal service delivery.
qs: At Harvey, we believe that the future of AI will not be a chatbot that compliments your workflow; it will be the platform your workflow is built on.
This is why we partner with entire firms.
These close collaborations allow us to find solutions for lawyers that go beyond training data and treatises.
You can't build self-driving cars in a lab and understanding the real problems faced by our clients is fundamental to making those problems AI-soluble.

kp.k: Legal AI trust requires review, feedback and secure systems
kp.d: The authors argue that Harvey must earn trust comparable to that underpinning law firms' and lawyers' reputations. They identify scalability, transparency and security as requirements, and describe tiered review, natural-language feedback, AI alignment and validation as mechanisms for building that trust. The announcement describes a development approach without supplying performance measurements or validation results.
qs: Law firms build their reputations on decades of being entrusted with their clients' most complex and critical problems.
To empower both, Harvey must build the same trust by developing AI systems that are not only powerful, but also scalable, transparent, and secure.

We do so by building systems that replicate historic best practices for establishing trust in knowledge work—such as tiered review and the ability to incorporate natural language feedback—while pioneering novel systems for AI alignment and validation.

kp.k: System development combines AI engineering and legal expertise
kp.d: The founders describe bringing AI research engineers and lawyers together to develop Harvey's systems. This identifies interdisciplinary development as part of their strategy for professional-services AI, rather than reporting changes to law-firm staffing structures or lawyers' training.
qs: To develop these cutting-edge systems, Harvey brings together engineers from the best AI research labs and lawyers from the most prestigious firms in the world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pereyra and Weinberg predict that large language models will augment knowledge workers rather than leave them without work, shifting their attention toward strategy, advice, and judgment.
pts.d: Writing as Harvey's founders, Gabe Pereyra and Winston Weinberg present GPT-4 as a change in how professional services are provided and consumed. They claim that language models can solve complex tasks efficiently and accurately, allowing professionals, including lawyers, to concentrate on judgment-intensive work. This is an augmentation claim, not a prediction of lawyer replacement.

pts.k: The authors predict that AI will become the platform underlying professional workflows rather than a supplementary chatbot.
pts.d: Pereyra and Weinberg link this prediction to Harvey's strategy of partnering with entire firms. They argue that close collaboration and understanding clients' actual problems are fundamental to developing AI solutions beyond what training data and legal treatises alone provide. The platform prediction does not explicitly entail autonomous legal practice.

pts.k: The authors argue that empowering lawyers and firms with AI requires trustworthy systems, and describe review, feedback, alignment, and validation as their approach.
pts.d: Harvey's founders identify scalability, transparency, and security alongside capability as requirements for earning professional trust. They say Harvey is building systems that reproduce practices such as tiered review and natural-language feedback while developing AI alignment and validation systems. These are stated development practices and conditions for empowerment, rather than demonstrated performance outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are supported by the founders' account of Harvey's development strategy and resources, not by reported outcome data or benchmarks.
pts.d: The authors cite firm partnerships, collaboration between AI engineers and lawyers, and review and feedback mechanisms as the practical basis for their vision. They report a $21 million Series A as resources for expanding the team, partnerships, and systems. The document supplies no quantified accuracy or efficiency results, employment evidence, named client case studies, or benchmark findings supporting the predicted effects. Its appended LawSites reference concerns the financing announcement; no findings from that coverage about AI's effects are reproduced.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 26, 2023 announcement presents GPT-4 as an immediate turning point but gives no deadline for the broader workflow transformation.
pts.d: The authors describe language-model benefits as potential and the platform model as their belief about the future. Firm partnerships and system-building are described as current activities. Achieving the envisioned transformation is linked to understanding real client problems, earning trust, developing capable and secure systems, and using the financing to expand resources. There is no quantified adoption timetable or forecast period.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers and entire law firms are the immediate focus, within a broader prediction about knowledge workers and professional services.
pts.d: Individual lawyers are expected to gain task-solving assistance and more scope for strategy, advice, and judgment. Firms are envisaged as partners whose workflows will be built on AI platforms, with trust and reputation central to implementation. Their clients are indirectly implicated through the provision of complex, critical services, but the authors do not specify changes in prices, access, or client outcomes. The source does not distinguish effects by lawyer seniority or firm size and does not predict particular staffing reductions.
